title: Transport stability: HTTP/2 multiplexing, HTTP/1 fallback, backpressure, and idempotent retries for SDKs
creator: Asha Patel
description: PRD-style ticket defining SDK-level requirements for robust transport behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go clients. Focus areas: prefer HTTP/2 multiplexing for low-latency concurrent requests, deterministic fallback to HTTP/1 when HTTP/2 is unavailable or broken, explicit backpressure semantics for streamed responses, and idempotent retry semantics for both unary and streaming endpoints.
background: Multiple customer incidents and internal benchmarks show that transport-layer mismatches (e.g., client forcing HTTP/1 single connection vs. server supporting HTTP/2 multiplex) lead to head-of-line blocking, increased tail latency, and surprising retry interactions. SDK teams have implemented ad-hoc solutions; we need a cross-language, product-level contract so applications built on Redwood Inference get predictable behavior.
goals: Define a single transport contract implemented consistently in Python/TS/Go SDKs
Ensure streaming APIs support natural backpressure and resume semantics without data corruption or duplicate events
Provide clear retry/idempotency guidance with default-safe policies and opt-in aggressive modes
Enable HTTP/2 multiplexing by default with a documented, observable fallback to HTTP/1
out_of_scope: Custom proxy appliances for enterprise customers (these will be handled as separate integration docs)
Protocol-level changes to existing API shapes (we assume current endpoints remain unchanged)
requirements: SDKs MUST attempt HTTP/2 ALPN negotiation on first connection to Redwood endpoints when platform support exists
If HTTP/2 negotiation fails, SDKs MUST fallback to HTTP/1 and document that fallback in telemetry
When using HTTP/2, SDKs MUST reuse a single multiplexed connection per host+port and limit concurrent streams according to client-side tunables (default: 50 streams)
When using HTTP/1 fallback, SDKs MUST use a configurable connection pool (default pool size: 8) and provide jittered exponential backoff for connection exhaustion
Streaming endpoints MUST expose a consumer-driven backpressure primitive: Python async iterator (.anext/.asend), TS async iterator/ReadableStream, Go io.Reader-like incremental API
Backpressure signals MUST pause reading from the socket (or slow consumer buffer) rather than dropping chunks; SDKs MUST honor flow-control windows where applicable
All streaming reconnects MUST be best-effort resumable: server-generated stream cursors or per-request checkpoints MUST be accepted by the server to resume from last acknowledged token
Unary requests and idempotent stream commands MUST support an idempotency key header; SDKs MUST include deterministic idempotency by default for retries on safe verbs

Default retry policy across SDKs: retry on transient network errors and 5xx server errors up to 3 attempts with exponential backoff and jitter; do NOT retry non-idempotent operations unless user enables aggressive mode
SDKs MUST expose observability hooks: transport_mode (http2/http1), fallback_reason, concurrent_streams, pool_exhausted, retry_count, last_retry_error
Authentication and token rotation MUST remain compatible with existing auth flows; transport changes MUST not require customers to change auth tokens
acceptance_criteria: Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs implement HTTP/2 negotiation and document the default behavior in README
Automated tests show that under simulated HTTP/2 failure, SDKs switch to HTTP/1 within 2s and emit fallback telemetry
End-to-end tests for streaming backpressure validate that slow consumers do not drop data and that flow-control windows are honored
Resume test: interrupted streams using server checkpoints resume without duplicate or missing tokens in >= 95% of trials across 50 simulated interruptions
Retry policy validated by integration tests: idempotent unary calls retried up to 3 times; non-idempotent calls are not retried by default
Telemetry metrics are ingested into staging Observability dashboard and show transport_mode, fallback_reason, and retry_count within 24h of SDK exercise
Docs and migration notes published in SDK repo and included in release notes for sdk-2026.04
design_notes: We will leverage existing HTTP client libraries per language: httpx/asyncio or aiohttp fallback in Python, fetch + http2-capable client in Node for TS (node: http2 or undici when available), and net/http + golang.org/x/net/http2 for Go. Each SDK will provide a transport abstraction layer so higher-level client code can remain unchanged when toggling backpressure or stream policies.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): implement and release experimental http2 transport in internal SDK packages and run integration tests against staging; collect telemetry for 1 week
Phase 2 (beta): ship to public prerelease packages, include migration docs, and allow opt-in via client config flag
Phase 3 (GA): flip defaults to prefer HTTP/2 and ship sdk-2026.04; keep HTTP/1 fallback enabled and monitored
Phase 4: follow-up: iterate on pool sizes and concurrent stream limits based on real-world telemetry
testing_plan: Unit tests for transport negotiation logic with mocked ALPN outcomes
Integration harness to simulate partial network partitions and validate fallback within SLA
Chaos tests for streaming resume using server-side checkpoint generator and random disconnects
Cross-language interoperability tests that open concurrent streams from each SDK and verify server-side ordering and lack of head-of-line blocking
Load tests exercising HTTP/1 connection pool limits to ensure graceful degradation
open_questions: What is the global default for concurrent HTTP/2 streams per SDK/runtime? (proposed 50)
How should SDKs surface client library limitations (e.g., Node http2 server vs client subtle differences) in the public API?
Do we need to provide a compatibility shim for older Node versions that lack stable http2 client APIs?
Should we allow automatic switching back to HTTP/2 after a fallback event, and if so, what cooldown/health checks are required?
decisions: Use per-language native HTTP/2 libraries where stable; do not implement a custom HTTP/2 stack
Default to HTTP/2 when the runtime supports it; fall back to HTTP/1 with telemetry and configurable pool sizes
Expose opt-in aggressive retry mode, disabled by default to avoid accidental duplicate side effects
